title: Tackling GPU Bottlenecks in Plane-Wave DFT with K-Point Batching and Mixed Precision | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA introduces Daviator, a batched k-point/spin GPU kernel library for VASP's Davidson eigensolver, plus a mixed-precision (FP32 with FP64 islands) layer; together they claim up to 22x faster and 60-75% cheaper (~$5-6M saved) generation of an OMat24-scale DFT dataset for MLIP training versus CPU, with the cheapest option on RTX PRO 6000. The piece frames FP64-stagnant GPU roadmaps as forcing HPC codes toward mixed precision.

themes.theme: DFT data demand for MLIP training

insights.claim: Training a next-generation machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) requires tens to hundreds of millions of density functional theory (DFT) calculations of energies, forces, and stresses.
insights.speaker: Erica Tsai
insights.so_what: AI-for-materials creates a massive, recurring HPC compute demand for ground-truth data generation.
insights.locator: Training a next-generation machine learning interatomic potential

insights.claim: Plane-wave DFT, with VASP as its dominant implementation, is described as the gold standard for generating MLIP training data and is ubiquitous at national labs and research institutions.
insights.speaker: Erica Tsai
insights.so_what: Accelerating VASP specifically captures the bulk of materials-science DFT compute spend.
insights.locator: Plane-wave DFT, with VASP as its

insights.claim: The Open Materials 2024 (OMat24) dataset contains over 100 million VASP data points from AIMD, rattled-relax, and rattled static calculations for MLIP training and validation.
insights.speaker: Erica Tsai
insights.so_what: Sizes the benchmark workload NVIDIA uses to argue GPU economics for scientific AI data generation.

themes.theme: Small-system GPU bottleneck and Daviator batching

insights.claim: VASP's OpenACC GPU port processes k-points sequentially, so for small systems with dense k-point grids kernel launch overhead dominates and a single-atom iron system with 752 k-points ran 8x slower on GPU than on CPU.
insights.speaker: Erica Tsai
insights.so_what: Shows that prior GPU ports left a large slice of DFT workloads better served by CPUs, a gap NVIDIA now targets.
insights.locator: Each k-point solve is largely independent

insights.claim: Daviator is an NVIDIA GPU kernel library that replaces sequential per-k-point processing with batched FFTs, GEMMs, and custom kernels in a batched Davidson eigensolver, raising SM occupancy from a fraction of capacity to near saturation while VASP keeps ownership of the SCF loop, mixing, symmetry, and I/O.
insights.speaker: Erica Tsai
insights.so_what: Software batching unlocks GPU utilization on workloads previously CPU-bound, expanding addressable GPU demand in HPC.
insights.locator: Daviator is a library of GPU

insights.claim: Daviator-enabled VASP delivers over 2x speed-up vs CPU on a single iron atom, a 22x Davidson speedup on LiFePO4 with r2SCAN, and more than 85% lower execution time on a 64-atom Bi-doped GaAs system, improving on prior state of the art at all system sizes.
insights.speaker: Erica Tsai
insights.so_what: Removes the need to route jobs between CPU and GPU by size, simplifying full migration of DFT fleets to GPUs.
insights.locator: Daviator overcomes the OpenACC port’s limitations

insights.claim: VASP with Daviator is currently limited to single-node execution, with multi-node support, non-collinear spin (vasp_ncl) and gamma-only (vasp_gam) coverage expected later.
insights.speaker: Erica Tsai
insights.so_what: Adoption limits for large-scale runs; watch for multi-node release as a trigger for broader uptake.
insights.locator: For now, VASP with Daviator is

insights.claim: Daviator and its mixed-precision option are distributed through the NVIDIA ALCHEMI VASP microservice, require a VASP user license, and work with existing VASP inputs by setting LDAVIATOR=True in the INCAR.
insights.speaker: Erica Tsai
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is packaging scientific software as microservices, tying ecosystem lock-in to its GPU platform.

insights.claim: FP64 throughput has held flat across NVIDIA Hopper, Blackwell, and Rubin data center GPUs while FP32 throughput keeps rising, and workstation GPUs like the RTX PRO 6000 have a 64:1 FP32:FP64 ratio.
insights.speaker: Erica Tsai
insights.so_what: Signals NVIDIA's roadmap deprioritizes FP64; HPC customers must adopt mixed precision or see stagnating effective throughput.
insights.locator: Additionally, plane-wave DFT traditionally runs in FP64

insights.claim: AI workloads are driving GPU hardware toward lower-precision data types, so the fraction of peak GPU throughput available to FP64-only HPC codes is stagnating.
insights.speaker: Erica Tsai
insights.so_what: Second-order effect of AI capex: traditional scientific computing must rewrite software to ride AI-optimized silicon.
insights.locator: Additionally, plane-wave DFT traditionally runs in FP64

insights.claim: Mixed-precision failures can be insidious: soft failures such as energy drift, incorrect convergence, or diverging MD trajectories can appear valid on casual inspection, so precision boundaries must be measured per kernel.
insights.speaker: Erica Tsai
insights.so_what: Validation tooling is a real barrier to mixed-precision adoption in scientific codes.
insights.quote: Soft failures are not: energy drift, incorrect convergence, diverging MD trajectories that appear valid on casual inspection.
insights.locator: Additionally, the failures can be insidious

insights.claim: NVIDIA proposes a precision-requirements workflow using a generic floating-point type with configurable mantissa and exponent bits, screening each kernel by lowering bits until results fail, with instrumentation possible at library (cuBLAS emulated GEMMs), language (NVIDIA CCCL type), or compiler (Verificarlo VPREC, CPU-only) levels.
insights.speaker: Erica Tsai
insights.so_what: A generalizable playbook for porting other HPC codes to lower precision, expanding the market for FP32-heavy GPUs.
insights.locator: The code instrumentation can be performed

insights.claim: In the mixed-precision Davidson solver, FFTs, Hamiltonian application, and orbital updates run in FP32 while the subspace eigenproblem, tall-skinny GEMMs, energies, and convergence measures stay in FP64, and a split-k algorithm breaks tall-skinny GEMMs into FP32 chunks with a final FP64 accumulation.
insights.speaker: Erica Tsai
insights.so_what: Illustrates the 'FP64 island' pattern that lets FP64-weak GPUs serve scientific workloads.
insights.locator: Following this workflow, the original analysis

insights.claim: On H100 and H200, where FP64 Tensor Cores match FP32 throughput, mixed precision gives only marginal end-to-end gains, whereas on the RTX PRO 6000 the FP32 Davidson solver runs 3x-7x faster for roughly 2x end-to-end acceleration.
insights.speaker: Erica Tsai
insights.so_what: Mixed precision shifts the cost-optimal hardware for HPC toward cheaper inference/workstation-class GPUs.
insights.locator: On H100 and H200, where FP64

insights.claim: On GaAsBi-64, FP32 gives a 2x speed-up at EDIFF = 10-5 eV and a combined FP32-then-FP64 run is 1.5x faster than pure FP64 at EDIFF = 10^-8 eV, since FP32 alone cannot converge below its noise floor.
insights.speaker: Erica Tsai
insights.so_what: Hybrid precision preserves accuracy while capturing speed, reducing scientific objections to adoption.

insights.claim: Projected over an OMat24-scale workload on the same number of cloud instances, VASP + Daviator is up to 22x faster than VASP on CPU nodes and up to 7x faster than VASP on GPU without Daviator, with the ALCHEMI microservice adding a further 3-5x throughput when batching eight small systems per GPU.
insights.speaker: Erica Tsai
insights.so_what: Projections from 13 benchmarked inputs; directionally strong case for GPU migration of DFT farms.
insights.locator: On the same number of cloud instances

insights.claim: Using a geometric mean of AWS, Azure, CoreWeave and Google on-demand prices, existing VASP OpenACC GPU support on datacenter GPUs is more expensive than CPU, but Daviator cuts cost to roughly 35% of CPU on H100/H200 and B200, and about 25% of CPU on RTX PRO 6000 with FP32.
insights.speaker: Erica Tsai
insights.so_what: Cheapest scientific compute lands on RTX PRO 6000 rather than flagship datacenter GPUs, relevant to cloud SKU mix and pricing.
insights.locator: To estimate the price of the data set

insights.claim: NVIDIA claims that for standard DFT GPUs are now the clear choice for VASP, with VASP + Daviator delivering 60-75% cost savings over CPU, or roughly $5-6M USD for an OMat24-sized dataset.
insights.speaker: Erica Tsai
insights.so_what: Pressure on CPU-based HPC procurement at labs and research institutions; tailwind for GPU cloud demand in scientific AI.
insights.quote: For standard DFT, GPUs are now the clear choice for VASP.

insights.claim: Daviator's speedups make meta-GGA functionals like R2SCAN viable for production, potentially bringing higher-accuracy DFT within reach for battery, catalyst, and defect datasets.
insights.speaker: Erica Tsai
insights.so_what: Higher-fidelity datasets could improve AI materials models for batteries and catalysts, an energy-transition adjacency.
